newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy govt, unions hammer out Euro-tax deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy govt, unions hammer out Euro-tax deal.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Tuesday hammered out a deal with trade unions over a 'Euro-tax' designed to whip Italy into shape for European monetary union, and deflected the threat of a general strike.
Prodi said the agreement represented the last piece in the puzzle before the lira can re-join the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) after four years of floating free.
"All the conditions are now in place for the re-entry of our currency into the ERM," Prodi told a news conference following his successful round of talks with union leaders.
The Euro-tax, which is made up of a packet of measures, aims to help Italy qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) at the start in 1999.
"It would be intolerable for Italy to be left out of monetary union," Prodi said.

The prime minister confirmed that the Euro tax would raise a total 12.5 trillion lire ($8.2 billion) next year, with 5.5 trillion lire of this coming from a one-off levy on income tax -- less than originally expected.

The rest of the money would come by bringing forward a tax on employees' severance payments, by demanding payment of taxes which have already fallen due and by negotiating more favourable terms for Italy's foreign currency debt.

Prodi said tax payers would be partially reimbursed, either through tax rebates starting from 1999, or else through privatisation options, giving Italians the right to buy shares in state companies which are slated for sell-off.

Italy's powerful unions warned at the weekend they would call a general strike over the Euro-tax and held five hours of talks with Prodi on Monday to try to soften the proposed measures. Following a fresh round of negotiations on Tuesday, they said they were now satisfied.
"This is a balanced package that takes into consideration union demands," Sergio D'Antoni, leader of the country's second largest union, told reporters.
However employers' group Confindustria and the opposition centre-right bloc said they were against the proposals.
"Not only will it not be a one-off measure, there probably won't be any reimbursements either," said former Finance Minister Giulio Tremonti.
The entire 1997 budget, which aims to cut 62.5 trillion lire off the deficit, was approved by the lower house of parliament on Saturday and has now moved to the upper house (Senate).

The government has always said that the lower house vote would be a milestone towards the lira's ERM re-entry and dismissed a report in an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that some European Union partners were worried about a swift return.
Daily Corriere della Sera said Germany and France were urging Italy to delay its ERM application until the year end when the Senate would have completed its reading of the bill.
"We have already said that with the approval of the budget in the lower house we can start talks," Prodi insisted.
The lira, which left the ERM in a currency crisis in September 1992, was unmoved by the comments, trading little changed from earlier at 1,006.75 per mark.
Prodi's six-month old centre-left coalition depends on the backing of the hardleft Communist Refoundation to control the lower house but enjoys a full majority in the upper house.
This should guarantee smooth passage in the Senate for the finance bill.
